evidence_quotes.quote: Results show that households are willing to pay a substantial increase in their water bills
Sampled households were randomly assigned one of the four treatments.
households prefer the current centralized administration over a potential decentralization

rationale: Full text read (14 pages). Vasquéz and Franceschi (2013) administer a contingent valuation survey of 690 urban households in León, Nicaragua, using a randomized 2x2 split-sample survey experiment ('experimental') that randomly assigns governance provider (centralized national utility ENACAL vs. decentralized municipal provision under Nicaragua's Law of Municipalities Article 7 and National Water Strategy) and water quality level (current vs. safe drinking water), alongside randomized monthly fee bids. The primary mechanism family is 'institutional_structure_coordination' (decentralization of water service mandate from a centralized national utility to municipal government), with 'fees_tariffs_subsidies' secondary as the monthly tariff/cost-recovery payment vehicle. The primary substantive access domain is 'effective_access' (24-hour service reliability/continuity, potability/water quality, and household coping with intermittent supply), while 'assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple' is 'multiple' because the study co-equally estimates household tariff willingness-to-pay and expenditure/income affordability shares ('economic_access') and citizen evaluations of institutional capacity, accountability, local knowledge, and governance preference between ENACAL and the municipality ('administrative_outcome').
